title: EV Grand Prix Electric Race Car
summary: An electric endurance car built and raced through electrical integration, telemetry, design, testing and team leadership.
overview: I head the school’s Electric Vehicle Grand Prix effort, coordinating more than 80 students across seven teams while working directly on the vehicle. We built and raced the car in 2026. My technical contributions span wiring and repairs, telemetry, battery and motor research, CAD and 3D scanning, race preparation and troubleshooting. The project continues toward the 2027 season.
contributions: Led and coordinated more than 80 students across seven teams.
Worked on vehicle wiring, soldering, electrical troubleshooting and repairs.
Developed the earlier telemetry integration and an AI-supported race strategy; finalized a revised telemetry design for 2027.
Contributed to battery and motor research, CAD, 3D scanning, body modelling and testing.
Worked with the driver during vehicle preparation and race-day checks.

technical.heading: A complete vehicle, not a single subsystem
technical.text: The car brings together a 48 V powertrain, controls, sensing, mechanical packaging and the team processes needed to test safely. Each change has to work with the rest of the vehicle, under constraints of mass, energy, reliability and race rules.

technical.heading: My hands-on role
technical.text: I wired and repaired electrical connections, investigated faults, worked on telemetry integration, supported CAD and body development, and prepared the car with the driver. Dedicated case studies explain the electrical system, telemetry, digital modelling and vehicle testing.

technical.heading: At the competition
technical.text: At Karting Town, Sharjah on 14 February 2026, the team received four EVGP awards. At the separate 2026 SABIS STEAM competition hosted at SIS Yas Island, the car placed third overall and was highest ranked in the Unmodified category.

results: EVGP 2026: 2nd place, Best Use of AI for Race Strategy
2026 SABIS STEAM competition at SIS Yas Island: 3rd place overall and highest ranked in the Unmodified category

title: EV Electrical & Powertrain
summary: The 48 V traction system, protection path, battery strategy and fault repairs behind the race car.
overview: I worked on the car’s power and control wiring and diagnosed faults during development. The 48 V traction system uses interchangeable packs of four 12 V / 12 Ah sealed lead-acid batteries in series. A separate 12.8 V / 7 Ah LiFePO4 pack powers low-voltage electronics and telemetry.
contributions: Wired, soldered and repaired vehicle electrical and control connections.
Traced a no-power failure to a blown main fuse and verified power after replacement.
Diagnosed and replaced a faulty contactor; repaired throttle and dashboard-control faults.
Proposed a one-pack-per-heat strategy to reduce the mass carried during each heat.

technical.heading: Protection and power path
technical.text: Traction power runs through an emergency kill switch, a 100 A fuse, contactor and precharge circuit before the motor controller and rear-wheel motor. A Cycle Analyst and shunt monitor the traction supply.

technical.heading: Throttle repair
technical.text: A damaged 14-pin connector interrupted the throttle signal. I bypassed the faulty connector, soldered the throttle wires to the correct controller connections and checked throttle response.

technical.heading: Dual-pack race strategy
technical.text: The plan is to install one interchangeable pack per heat and swap between heats. This reduces mass carried during each run while keeping both packs available across the competition. The expected efficiency benefit is a design rationale, not a measured race result.

technical.heading: Verification after repair
technical.text: I checked continuity, voltage and the affected function after each repair, then repeated the original fault test before returning to wider vehicle testing.

results: 48 V vehicle power system built and tested
Main-fuse, contactor, throttle and dashboard faults diagnosed and repaired

title: EV Telemetry System
summary: Vehicle measurement work and a finalized ESP32-C3 / Raspberry Pi architecture planned for the 2027 car.
overview: Telemetry has been my main individual technical focus on the EV. I integrated and tested an earlier measurement setup on the car, tracing power, grounding, continuity, communication and signal-quality issues. I later finalized a revised architecture for planned use in 2027. The revised hardware was a design at the 2026 race.
contributions: Connected the telemetry system to the vehicle's electrical system.
Tested voltage, current, speed and location measurement channels separately.
Checked sensor power, grounding, wiring continuity and communication between hardware components.
Reduced interference by shielding and reorganizing signal wiring, then retested readings on the car.
Finalized the 2027 architecture around sensing, local processing and remote connectivity.

technical.heading: 2026 vehicle integration
technical.text: For the earlier system, I checked sensor power, grounding, wiring continuity and communication between components. I tested voltage, current, speed and location channels individually before checking them together on the car. Shielding and signal-wire routing helped address interference and inaccurate readings, including issues affecting the Cycle Analyst.

technical.heading: What the data is for
technical.text: The measurement plan covers pack voltage, battery current, speed and vehicle position. Logged or transmitted readings could help the team compare tests, understand energy use and make better-informed race decisions.

technical.heading: Finalized 2027 design
technical.text: The revised architecture specifies an ESP32-C3 for sensing and low-level communication, an ADS1115 ADC, a Raspberry Pi 4B for processing, a cellular/GNSS module, a voltage-divider circuit and Hall-effect current sensing. This design is finalized for planned use on the 2027 car.

technical.heading: Design iteration
technical.text: The earlier ESP32-based approach was simpler. The revised design separates sensing, processing and connectivity. IMU and wheel-Hall concepts were removed after the measurement plan was narrowed to what GPS could provide.

results: Earlier telemetry system integrated and tested on the EV
Revised system design finalized for planned use in 2027

title: EV CAD & Reverse Engineering
summary: Scanning the existing race car, then revising its digital body shape for a more streamlined design.
overview: Our team scanned the existing electric race car and turned the physical body into a 3D mesh. That original model became the starting point for an edited body shape intended to be more aerodynamic. I contributed to the scanning, mesh review and CAD work. The gallery shows both stages; the revised shape is a design iteration, not a measured drag result.
contributions: Contributed to the 3D scan and digital model of the existing race car.
Reviewed the original mesh to understand the body and component space.
Helped develop an edited body model with a more streamlined shape for design review.

technical.heading: From car to model
technical.text: The workflow moved from the physical car to a 3D scan and mesh. The original model preserved the existing body shape and gave the team geometry to inspect before making changes.

technical.heading: Body-shape revision
technical.text: We then edited the digital body to explore a more streamlined exterior while checking how the revised shape related to the original car. The side, front and three-quarter views document that design step.

technical.heading: Scope of evidence
technical.text: The gallery separates the original scan from the revised body model. These screenshots document the design process; they do not by themselves establish a measured aerodynamic gain.

results: Original 3D scan and revised body model documented in multiple views

title: EV Mechanical Design & Testing
summary: Packaging, material choices, airflow study and repeatable fault-finding on the electric race car.
overview: I contributed to mechanical decisions and testing across the EV project, including floorboard materials, weight, steering layout, battery mounting, braking components and overall packaging. I also used a CFD airflow visualization to examine the existing body and explore a smoother shape in CAD.
contributions: Supported mechanical packaging and material-selection discussions.
Reviewed an airflow visualization from a CFD model of the race car.
Used testing and fault diagnosis to guide vehicle changes and repairs.

technical.heading: Vehicle packaging
technical.text: A small endurance car forces close coordination between steering, motor, batteries, controls, brakes and the driver. Decisions about one part affect mass distribution, access for repair and available space elsewhere.

technical.heading: Airflow study
technical.text: A 3D representation of the vehicle was used in CFD to visualize airflow around the body. Disrupted regions suggested possible geometry changes, which were explored in CAD. The visualization is a simulation, not a measured on-track aerodynamic result.

technical.heading: Repeat the original test
technical.text: For electrical and control faults, the team traced the failure, changed the suspect part or connection, then repeated the same test to confirm the fault was actually resolved.

results: CFD visualization used to inform body-design discussion
Vehicle tests and post-repair checks supported further iteration
